title: Decision Trees I - Intuition and Structure
abstract:
A decision tree is nothing but a nested if-else statement, learned from data
rather than written by hand. This document covers the anatomy — root node,
decision nodes, leaf nodes — how a tree partitions the feature space into
axis-aligned boxes, the split between classification trees (focused on class
purity) and regression trees (focused on error minimisation), the greedy
recursive algorithm that builds one, and the properties that make trees unlike
every model so far: no scaling needed, native handling of categorical features,
complete interpretability, and a strong tendency to overfit.

blocks.t: What a Decision Tree Is
From the notes
A decision tree is nothing but an if-else statement.

The notes' example, and the code it is equivalent to. The tree
 is the program — the only difference from hand-written logic is that
 the conditions and their order were learned from data.

blocks.t: How a Tree Sees the Feature Space

blocks.cap:
Each split is a single condition on a single feature, so it is a
 horizontal or vertical cut. The result is a partition of the space into
 axis-aligned rectangles, and the decision boundary is a staircase.

blocks.t: The geometric picture, and what follows from it

A tree partitions the feature space into axis-aligned boxes, and predicts
a constant inside each box. Four consequences, all of them important:

items:
No feature scaling is needed. A split asks
 "is $x_j \le c$?", which depends only on the ordering of that
 feature's values. Any monotone rescaling leaves the tree unchanged
 (Topics 13–14).

Interactions come free. Splitting on $x_1$ and then on $x_2$
 within one branch expresses "the effect of $x_2$ depends on $x_1$"
 without you constructing anything.

Diagonal boundaries are expensive. A boundary at
 $x_1+x_2=5$ must be approximated by a staircase, needing many splits.
 This is the mirror image of a linear model's strength.

No extrapolation. Outside the training range the prediction is
 whatever the nearest leaf says — a flat constant. A tree can never
 predict a value above the largest target it saw.

From the notes

Regression \newline [focus on error minimization]
rows: 3. Choose the split with min error
4. Choose best split based on feature IG
5. Repeat until all nodes are pure

blocks.cap:
Left: the two variants side by side. Right: a regression tree predicts
 a constant within each leaf, so its output is a step function — and deeper
 trees simply produce more, narrower steps.

blocks.t: The two differ only in the split criterion

The recursive procedure is identical; only the measure of a "good" split
changes. Classification asks how pure are the child nodes? and answers with
entropy or Gini (Topic 55). Regression asks how small is the error? and
answers with variance or MSE. Everything else — greedy search, stopping rules,
pruning — is shared.
The Algorithm
Recursive greedy partitioning

items:
At the current node with data $S$, consider every feature $j$ and every
 candidate threshold $c$.

Each candidate splits $S$ into $S_L=\{x: x_j\le c\}$ and
 $S_R=\{x: x_j>c\}$.

Score the split by the weighted impurity of the children:
 $$\text{cost}(j,c)=\frac{|S_L|}{|S|}I(S_L)+\frac{|S_R|}{|S|}I(S_R)$$
 where $I$ is entropy or Gini for classification, variance or MSE for
 regression.
Take the $(j,c)$ minimising that cost. Recurse on each child.
Stop when the node is pure, or a stopping rule fires (Topic 57).

blocks.t: Greedy, and why

The algorithm picks the best split at each node in isolation, never
reconsidering. It is therefore greedy and not guaranteed to find the
globally optimal tree — a worse first split can sometimes enable two excellent
second splits.

Finding the optimal tree is NP-complete, so greedy search is the practical
compromise. This also explains why trees are unstable: a small change in
the data can change the root split, and every subtree below it changes with it.
That instability is exactly what bagging exploits (Topic 60).
How candidate thresholds are chosen

For a numerical feature, sort the unique values and consider midpoints between
consecutive ones — at most $n-1$ candidates per feature. The optimum can only
lie between two observed values, so nothing is lost. This makes the cost of one
node $O(np\log n)$, and the whole tree roughly $O(np\log^2 n)$.
Properties

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Works with both categorical and numerical features
Overfits — a fully grown tree memorises the training set
Performs poorly on imbalanced data — splits chase the majority class
Completely interpretable — you can read the rules
Unstable: a small data change can restructure the whole tree
Fast to train and to predict

blocks.t: Why a fully grown tree always overfits

Left unconstrained, the algorithm keeps splitting until every leaf is pure — in
the limit, one leaf per training row. Training accuracy is then 100% and the tree
has learned the noise as thoroughly as the signal.

Two families of fixes, both in Topic 57: pre-pruning (stop early with
max_depth, min_samples_leaf) and post-pruning (grow
fully, then cut back). And the ensemble methods of Topics 58–70 exist largely
because a single tree, however pruned, remains high-variance.
Why imbalanced data hurts

The impurity measures reward reducing the weighted impurity, and with a
99/1 split a node is already almost pure before any split. There is little
impurity to remove, so the tree finds no reason to isolate the minority class.
The standard fixes are class_weight="balanced" and the resampling methods
of Topic 80.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. IT REALLY IS AN IF-ELSE STATEMENT
# =====================================================================
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "occupation": rng.choice(["student", "engineer", "doctor"], 400),
    "gender":     rng.choice(["male", "female"], 400),
})
app = np.where(df.occupation == "student", "PUBG",
      np.where(df.gender == "female", "GitHub", "WhatsApp"))

X = pd.get_dummies(df).astype(int)
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, app)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns)))
# The printed tree IS the if-else logic, recovered from data alone.
print("training accuracy:", tree.score(X, app))       # 1.0 -- the rule is exact

# =====================================================================
# 2. NO FEATURE SCALING REQUIRED
# =====================================================================
n = 1000
Xn = np.c_[rng.uniform(20, 60, n), rng.uniform(20_000, 200_000, n)]
yn = (Xn[:, 0] > 40).astype(int)                      # truth depends on AGE only
Xz = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xn)

t_raw    = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xn, yn)
t_scaled = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xz, yn)
print(f"\ntree raw    accuracy {t_raw.score(Xn, yn):.4f}")
print(f"tree scaled accuracy {t_scaled.score(Xz, yn):.4f}")
print("identical predictions:",
      np.array_equal(t_raw.predict(Xn), t_scaled.predict(Xz)))
# A split is a threshold on ONE feature, so only the ORDER matters.
print("logistic raw vs scaled:",
      round(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=500), Xn, yn, cv=5).mean(), 3),
      round(cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=500), Xz, yn, cv=5).mean(), 3))

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE GREEDY SPLIT SEARCH, IMPLEMENTED
# =====================================================================
def gini(y):
    if len(y) == 0: return 0.0
    p = np.bincount(y, minlength=2) / len(y)
    return 1 - (p ** 2).sum()

def best_split(X, y):
    """Try every feature and every midpoint; return the lowest weighted impurity."""
    best = (np.inf, None, None)
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        vals = np.unique(X[:, j])
        for c in (vals[:-1] + vals[1:]) / 2:          # midpoints only
            L = X[:, j] <= c
            if L.sum() == 0 or (~L).sum() == 0:
                continue
            cost = L.mean() * gini(y[L]) + (~L).mean() * gini(y[~L])
            if cost < best[0]:
                best = (cost, j, c)
    return best

Xg = np.c_[rng.uniform(0, 10, 300), rng.uniform(0, 10, 300)]
yg = ((Xg[:, 0] > 6) | ((Xg[:, 1] > 7) & (Xg[:, 0] < 3))).astype(int)
cost, j, c = best_split(Xg, yg)
print(f"\nscratch best split: feature {j} <= {c:.4f}  (weighted gini {cost:.4f})")

sk = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(Xg, yg)
print(f"sklearn root split: feature {sk.tree_.feature[0]} <= "
      f"{sk.tree_.threshold[0]:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. AXIS-ALIGNED SPLITS -- diagonals are expensive
# =====================================================================
Xd = rng.uniform(0, 10, (2000, 2))
y_axis = (Xd[:, 0] > 5).astype(int)                   # axis-aligned truth
y_diag = (Xd[:, 0] + Xd[:, 1] > 10).astype(int)       # DIAGONAL truth

print(f"\n{'max_depth':>10s} {'axis-aligned':>14s} {'diagonal':>11s}")
for d in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]:
    a = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0),
                        Xd, y_axis, cv=5).mean()
    b = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0),
                        Xd, y_diag, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{d:10d} {a:14.4f} {b:11.4f}")
print(f"{'logistic':>10s} "
      f"{cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), Xd, y_axis, cv=5).mean():14.4f} "
      f"{cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), Xd, y_diag, cv=5).mean():11.4f}")
# Depth 1 solves the axis-aligned problem. The diagonal needs depth 8+ to
# approximate what logistic regression gets with a single line.

# =====================================================================
# 5. REGRESSION TREES -- a step function, and no extrapolation
# =====================================================================
xr = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, 200))
yr = np.sin(xr * .8) * 3 + xr * .4 + rng.normal(0, .5, 200)

reg = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(xr[:, None], yr)
print(f"\nregression criterion: {reg.criterion}")          # 'squared_error'
print(f"leaves: {reg.get_n_leaves()}   distinct predictions: "
      f"{len(np.unique(reg.predict(xr[:, None])))}")
# One constant per leaf -- the output is a STEP FUNCTION.

far = np.array([[20.0], [50.0], [100.0]])
print(f"far outside the training range: {reg.predict(far).round(3)}")
print(f"largest training target: {yr.max():.3f}")
# All identical, and bounded by what it saw. A tree cannot extrapolate.

# =====================================================================
# 6. IT OVERFITS -- and imbalance makes it worse
# =====================================================================
Xo = rng.normal(0, 1, (600, 8))
yo = (Xo[:, 0] + Xo[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1.2, 600) > 0).astype(int)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xo, yo, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

print(f"\n{'max_depth':>10s} {'leaves':>8s} {'train':>8s} {'test':>8s} {'gap':>8s}")
for d in [1, 2, 4, 8, None]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    tr, te = t.score(Xtr, ytr), t.score(Xte, yte)
    print(f"{str(d):>10s} {t.get_n_leaves():8d} {tr:8.4f} {te:8.4f} {tr-te:8.4f}")
# Unconstrained: 1.000 on training -- one leaf per row.

Xi = rng.normal(0, 1, (4000, 6))
yi = (rng.random(4000) < 1/(1+np.exp(-(2.5*Xi[:, 0] - 5.0)))).astype(int)
Xitr, Xite, yitr, yite = train_test_split(Xi, yi, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=yi, random_state=0)
print(f"\npositive rate {yi.mean():.2%}")
for cw in [None, "balanced"]:
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, class_weight=cw,
                               random_state=0).fit(Xitr, yitr)
    print(f"class_weight={str(cw):>9s}  accuracy {t.score(Xite, yite):.4f}  "
          f"recall {recall_score(yite, t.predict(Xite)):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. INSTABILITY -- one changed row can restructure the tree
# =====================================================================
print("\nroot split across bootstrap samples:")
for s in range(6):
    idx = np.random.default_rng(s).choice(len(Xtr), len(Xtr), replace=True)
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr[idx], ytr[idx])
    print(f"  sample {s}: feature {t.tree_.feature[0]} <= "
          f"{t.tree_.threshold[0]:+.3f}")
# The ROOT changes between samples, and everything below it changes too.
# This high variance is exactly what bagging exploits (Topic 60).

# =====================================================================
# 8. READING A FITTED TREE
# =====================================================================
t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("\n", export_text(t, feature_names=[f"x{i}" for i in range(8)], max_depth=2))
print(f"depth {t.get_depth()}   leaves {t.get_n_leaves()}   "
      f"nodes {t.tree_.node_count}")
print("feature importances:", t.feature_importances_.round(3))
# Every prediction is fully traceable: follow the conditions down to a leaf.
# No other model in this course is this transparent.
Worked Examples
Choosing the root split for a placement dataset
Ten students. Feature: has internship (Y/N). Label: placed (yes/no). Counts:
Step 1 – impurity of the root. With $p=0.5$:
Step 2 – impurity of each child. Both children have $p = 0.8$ (or $0.2$ for the placed fraction, which gives the same impurity):
\text{Entropy}_{\text{child}} = -0.8\log_2 0.8 - 0.2\log_2 0.2 = 0.722
Step 3 – weighted impurity after the split. Each child holds half the rows, so the weighted impurity is the same as the child value: $0.32$ (Gini), $0.722$ (entropy).
Step 4 – information gain.
\text{Gain}_{\text{Gini}} = 0.50 - 0.32 = 0.18, \qquad \text{Gain}_{\text{Entropy}} = 1.000 - 0.722 = 0.278

Interpretation. The internship split removes 18 points of Gini impurity. A tree would compare this gain with every other feature and threshold, and take the largest. The two criteria usually pick the same split; they differ mainly in how they treat very uneven splits.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
A decision tree is nothing but an if-else statement, with the
 conditions learned from data.

Anatomy: root node (first question), decision nodes
 (internal questions), leaf nodes (predictions).

It can work with both categorical and numerical features, and is
 a supervised technique used for classification and regression.

Disadvantage: it overfits, and performs poorly on imbalanced
 data.

Every split is a threshold on one feature, so the tree partitions the
 space into axis-aligned boxes. Hence: no scaling needed,
 interactions free, diagonal boundaries expensive, no extrapolation.

Classification focuses on class purity: entropy or Gini
 check $\to$ split on features $\to$ information gain $\to$ best split
 $\to$ repeat until nodes are pure.

Regression focuses on error minimisation: try each
 feature $\to$ compute error after each split $\to$ choose the minimum
 $\to$ repeat.

The algorithm is greedy — best split at each node, never
 reconsidered — which is why trees are unstable, and why bagging works.

A fully grown tree reaches 100% training accuracy by memorising. Fix with
 pruning (Topic 57) or ensembles (Topics 58–70).

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why don't decision trees need feature scaling?

Because a split is a threshold on a single feature — "is $x_j\le c$?" — so
only the ordering of that feature's values matters. Any monotone rescaling maps
the thresholds along with the data and leaves the tree identical. Distance- and
gradient-based models have no such property.
Q. Why does a decision tree overfit so easily?

Because unconstrained it keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, which in the
limit means one leaf per training row. It has enough capacity to memorise the
noise exactly, and nothing in the objective discourages it.
Q. What does it mean that the algorithm is greedy?

It chooses the best split at each node in isolation and never revisits it. Finding
the globally optimal tree is NP-complete, so this is a practical compromise — but
it means a worse first split that would enable two excellent later splits is never
found.
Q. Why are trees unstable?

Because the greedy search means a small change in the data can flip the root
split, and every subtree beneath it is then rebuilt on different data. High
variance is the defining weakness of a single tree — and precisely what bagging
and random forests are designed to average away.
Q. Can a decision tree extrapolate?

No. Every prediction is a constant learned in some leaf, so the output is bounded
by the training targets. Ask it to price a house twice the size of anything it has
seen and it returns the value of the largest leaf it knows.
Q. Why do trees struggle with a diagonal boundary?

Splits are axis-aligned, so a boundary like $x_1+x_2=5$ must be approximated by a
staircase of horizontal and vertical cuts. It needs many splits and many rows,
where a linear model draws it with one line. This is the exact mirror of the
tree's advantage on axis-aligned structure.
